If Claim 2 is granted in full, all PH-authorized explorations and extractions of minerals, oil, and natural resources in the West Philippine Sea would be legally justified
If Claim 3 is granted in full, the Philippines would exercise and enjoy maritime, fishing, ecologic, and other rights within and beyond its EEZ and CS
No amount of artificial reclamation work can change the status of low-tide elevations or submerged banks -- they remain incapable of generating maritime entitlements

China refused to participate but published a Dec 7, 2014 Position Paper, wrote many diplomatic Notes Verbales, and sent two letters to Tribunal members, arguing no jurisdiction and preferring bilateral negotiations -- but did not express any position on substantive issues

The Tribunal nonetheless provided China with eight due-process safeguards -- prompt delivery of communications, adequate time to respond, invitations to comment on procedural steps, adequate notice of hearings, prompt provision of transcripts, Registry-Embassy availability for questions, and a standing invitation to participate at any stage
Will our people celebrate again when they receive the Tribunal's decision next year? Abangan!

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains the unanimous Oct 29, 2015 'Award on Jurisdiction and Admissibility' of the 'Arbitral Tribunal constituted under Annex VII to the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea' upholding the Tribunal's jurisdiction over the case filed by the Philippines against China. Our people have every reason to celebrate: had the Tribunal ruled otherwise, the arbitration would have ended immediately as a dismal defeat -- China would have completely won in absentia. Awards are final; unlike in our country, no MR or appeal to any other international tribunal or court is possible. Having assumed jurisdiction, the Tribunal will hold further hearings to decide on the merit. Contrary to some commentators, the Tribunal -- even after assuming jurisdiction -- will not render any decision granting territorial rights to either party; it cannot award ownership over any island or isle claimed or occupied by either side; in fact, the Philippines -- conscious of this limitation -- is not asking for any ruling on 'territorial aspects.' The 151-page Award also explains clearly the respective positions of the parties and how the merits hearing will be conducted. The PH 'Memorial' of June 30, 2014 sets out 15 submissions consolidated into three basic claims. First, the PH 'seeks declarations that the Parties' respective rights and obligations in regard to the waters, seabed, and maritime features of the South China Sea are governed by UNCLOS and that China's claims based on historic rights encompassed within its so-called nine-dash line are inconsistent with Convention and therefore invalid.' (CJ comment: if granted in full, China's omnibus claims over the entire SCS would be illegal under international law; the US sailing a warship within 12 nm of a Chinese-occupied isle signaled conformity to this claim.) Second, the PH 'seeks determination as to whether, under the Convention, certain maritime features claimed by both China and the Philippines are properly characterized as islands, rocks, low tide elevations, or submerged banks.' Islands generate EEZ + CS up to 200 nm; rocks generate territorial sea up to 12 nm; low-tide elevations and submerged banks generate nothing -- and no amount of artificial reclamation can change the status. (CJ comment: if granted in full, all PH-authorized resource explorations and extractions in the WPS would be legally justified.) Third, the PH 'seeks declarations that China has violated the Convention by interfering with the exercise of the Philippines' sovereign rights and freedoms under the Convention and through constructions and fishing activities that have harmed the marine environment.' (CJ comment: if granted in full, the PH would exercise and enjoy maritime, fishing, ecologic, and other similar rights within and beyond its economic zone and continental shelf.) China consistently refused to participate but published a Position Paper dated Dec 7, 2014, wrote many diplomatic Notes Verbales, and sent two letters to Tribunal members, all arguing that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction and that the solution is 'bilateral negotiations and friendly consultations.' China stressed it would not be bound by any decision but did not express any position on the substantive issues. Nonetheless, the Tribunal (a) ensured all communications were promptly delivered to China; (b) granted adequate time to respond; (c) invited comment on procedural steps; (d) provided adequate notice of hearings; (e) promptly provided transcripts of the Hearing on Jurisdiction and all documents submitted; (f) invited comment on anything said during the hearings; (g) made Registry staff available to the Chinese Embassy for any question; (h) reiterated that it remains open to China to participate at any stage. Will our people celebrate again when they receive the Tribunal's decision next year? Abangan! In a postscript clarification re his prior column 'Going for the jugular,' CJ notes that SolGen Hilbay says he would 'really love the chance of crossing swords with' former SolGen Estelito P. Mendoza, but the SBN law requires the OMB's Special Prosecutor (not the SolGen) to defend SBN decisions in the SC.
